# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Report

Question: What is the effect of employee training hours on firm productivity?

Approach: OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I control for firm size, firm age, the pre-period value of the outcome and mgmt_rating_2023, which captures an important determinant of the outcome, and trim the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on training_hours is -2.142 (SE 0.221, p = 0.0000, N = 1960).

Conclusion: negative effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.

import pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
d=pd.read_csv('data.csv')
pre='log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020'
full=pre+'+export_share_2020+foreign_owned+family_owned+rd_intensity_2020+union_share_2020+credit_score_2020+C(region)+listed+C(sector)'
for n,f in [('none','productivity_2023~training_hours'),('pre','productivity_2023~training_hours+'+pre),('full','productivity_2023~training_hours+'+full),('full+m','productivity_2023~training_hours+'+full+'+mgmt_rating_2023')]:
    r=smf.ols(f,d).fit(cov_type='HC1');print(n,r.params['training_hours'],r.bse['training_hours'])
print(smf.ols('mgmt_rating_2023~training_hours+'+full,d).fit().params['training_hours'])
E

content.text:
I rejected the report. I wrote `verdict.json` with `"decision": "reject"`.

The negative result depends on one control, `mgmt_rating_2023`. That rating comes from the 2023 survey, so it was measured after the training period. Training and productivity can both affect it, so controlling for it can distort the training estimate.

I re-ran the regression with different control sets. These are the training-hours coefficients, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors:

| Controls | Coefficient | SE |
|---|---|---|
| None | +2.49 | 0.24 |
| Pre-period controls only | +0.59 | 0.23 |
| Pre-period controls plus the other 2020 firm characteristics, region, listing and sector | +0.58 | 0.23 |
| Same set plus `mgmt_rating_2023` | −2.35 | 0.23 |

The sign flips from positive to negative only when the 2023 rating is added. The analyst's −2.14 uses a smaller control set plus that rating, and also trims the top and bottom 1% of productivity. I did not re-run that exact specification.

I also checked that the rating responds to both variables. After controlling for the 2020 characteristics, it rises with training hours (+0.66) and with 2023 productivity (+0.06).
